As far as the coding user experience that I have personally observed, game programming peaked with the team developing NBA Inside Drive 2004 for the Xbox.

Their workflow was:

1) Arrive at work. Get coffee. Fetch latest code from Visual Source Safe.

2) Turn on Xbox. Hit F5 to build, deploy and start debugging on target.

3) Edit and Continue C++ in debugger IDE all day on target without ever bothering to stop the game. (Yes, this took some coding discipline to maintain.)

4) Turn off Xbox and go home.

Between the Visual Studio debugger and the Whole Tomato coding assistance, it was easy to understand the code and the runtime behavior. For anything GPU-related, Microsoft Pix for Xbox gave you a scrubbable timeline of every action, every pixel, every register change in the GPU while drawing a frame.

The hardware capabilities, available libraries, and artist tools have increased tremendously since then. But, the coding experience has not. 20 years later, I'm outside of gaming and I find most people using re-run-and-printf debugging for professional development. Even locally. I don't know how anyone gets anything done.

The only significant improvements I've seen in 20 years (besides the occasional memory tracker or profiler tool) has been AI agents and reversible debuggers. Otherwise, it's all been downhill since 2004.

jdw64 · Nov 13, 2026

I'm not sure if the software is really the same, but there are a lot of AI slop games, and also a lot of well-made AI games. The graphical improvement in recently successful indie games is astonishing. Realistically speaking, in the past there were many cases where people weren't good at shaders, but there are also many points where optimization has improved. At the art asset level, even if AI isn't used, there are many cases where the code is now far better optimized than before. When I decompile the recent code of indie games whose animation implementation was terrible in the past, I often find it genuinely impressive.

Realistically speaking, AI raised the average quality. Among today's AI slop games, there are many that would have been "at this level of quality, this game could succeed" in the past.

Realistically, that's how it is. So there will be many people telling bad-luck stories like "ever since AI came out, GitHub has stalled," but I think that's closer to the opposite — AI increased production so much that the supply chain itself can't keep up.

The thing is, I can't really agree with the claim that software is the same. I don't know about open source, but when I think about the state of code in code delivered to clients, I think there has been a dramatic rise. Separately from that, because products are pouring out, I think consumers' quality demands are rising far faster than production. Comparing early smartphone games with today's AI slop games makes this even more palpable.
